annotationRationale: The main method counts exhaustive, disjoint cases by opposite pairs and uses parity to reject impossible cases. The distinct alternative branches on one person's partner and derives a recurrence. Both reviewed shared-bank methods are retained with their original reference credits.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is appropriate. No area repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: Independently counting by the number of opposite pairs gives counts 2, 5, 0, 5, 0, 1, totaling 13. This agrees with choice C and the key. The stem is consistent, no figures are supplied, and there is no grading-status conflict.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: For the identical 2020_AMC_10B_Q17, count-opposite-pairs and fix-one-partner-and-recur are both retained and independently valid. Historical opposite-pair-parity is merged into count-opposite-pairs. Historical opposite-pair-congruences is omitted because it reformulates the same parity obstruction without adding a distinct route; no worked explanation is supplied. Historical ladder-recurrence is merged into fix-one-partner-and-recur. The current LIVE argument and AoPS Solution 1 support the first route. AoPS Solution 2 is correctly omitted: knowing three people does not imply membership in a four-person group whose members all know one another. No additional accessible route is needed.
review.annotationCheck: The assessed cnm_h230 correctly identifies the central disjoint-case counting skill used by both methods. Parity remains explicitly mapped in the first method, and graph modeling and recurrence remain specific to the alternative. The empty support and context lists introduce no incorrect role assignments.
review.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is appropriate. No area repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: All six cases are correct. With no opposite pairs there are two alternating neighbor matchings; one opposite pair gives five uniquely completed choices. Two opposite pairs leave three people on each separated side, preventing neighbor-only completion. For three opposite pairs, the two unused diameters must be consecutive modulo five, giving exactly the five listed choices, including the wraparound case. Four opposite pairs force a fifth, while all five give one matching. The cases are exhaustive and disjoint, so the total is 13.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Correctly credits amc/2020_AMC_10B_Q17#count-opposite-pairs and retains both inherited IDs, live-reference-2020_AMC_10B_Q17 and aops-reference-2020_AMC_10B_Q17. The current LIVE and AoPS Solution 1 citations support the same classification. The source-informed-original basis accurately identifies permitted project-method reuse informed by nonofficial sources. No third-party sentence copying is apparent.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The opening explains why opposite-pair casework fits. Unique completion of even blocks is justified, the table explains every count, and the detailed three-opposite-pair discussion handles cyclic adjacency explicitly. A learner can reconstruct the argument without a diagram.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: Both immediate IDs are supported: cnm_h230 captures disjoint-case addition, and cnm_p156 captures the parity obstruction. The derived block-pairing consequences require no additional catalog node.

nativeLayerJudgments.CN: The supplied exact CN native-topic links for addition counting and odd/even numbers fit the argument. This application does not establish full coverage of a national standard.
nativeLayerJudgments.US: The supplied partial 2.OA.C.3 link for cnm_p156 fits parity through pairing, but the full standard is not assessed. No accepted US link is supplied for cnm_h230.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: The two concepts precisely support the written classification and impossibility arguments. Neither graph terminology nor modular arithmetic is needed as a separate immediate concept.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The ladder decomposition correctly gives L_m=L_(m-1)+L_(m-2), with L_0=L_1=1 and hence L_3=3, L_4=5. Pairing 0 with 5 leaves exactly a four-column ladder. Pairing 0 with 1 forces 5 to choose 4 or 6: choosing 6 leaves a three-column ladder, while choosing 4 forces (6,7), (2,3), and (8,9). Thus this branch contributes four. Reflection gives four for partner 9, and the disjoint partner branches total 5+4+4=13.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: Correctly credits amc/2020_AMC_10B_Q17#fix-one-partner-and-recur and retains both inherited LIVE and AoPS reference IDs. The recurrence is honestly presented as development within the reviewed project method, rather than as an official MAA argument. The source-informed-original basis and permitted project-explanation reuse are appropriate.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The explanation motivates branching on one partner, defines the auxiliary ladder arrangement, proves its recurrence and initial values, and identifies the residual rows explicitly. The forced branch and reflection are sufficiently explained for an AMC 12 learner.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: All three immediate IDs fit: math:graph-models represents the allowed connections, cnm_h230 combines disjoint branches, and math:recursive-counting-probability captures construction of the finite ladder recurrence with initial conditions.
